title: 4.6.1 Phases, gates, and the safety stream
pars: The seven phases fall into three groups (Figure 4.1). Preparation covers feasibility and start-up, conduct covers enrollment, surgery, and follow-up, and closure covers close-out and continuous improvement. Feasibility is the site’s own assessment of whether it can conduct the investigation, which informs the sponsor’s selection and covers CtQ domain 1. Start-up sets up the four pillars before any participant data exist, from training and credentialing, domain 6, to the reception and storage of the device. Enrollment covers participant selection and consent, domains 2 and 3, surgery covers device management and procedural delivery, domains 4 and 5, and follow-up covers domains 7, 8, and 9, from retention to the assessment of outcomes and images. Data capture and deviation management, domains 11 and 12, run through every phase.

The phases of preparation and closure belong to the site and follow one another, and each ends when its exit condition is met, which the PI confirms at a milestone review before the next phase opens. The phases of conduct belong to each participant, so one participant may be in screening while another is already in follow-up, and for the site each of them opens with its first case and closes with its last. The passage that carries most weight is the end of start-up, when the site confirms that it is ready to enroll and records the level at which it implements the framework (Section 4.7).

Safety surveillance runs as a stream across the phases of conduct, from the first enrolled participant to the last follow-up assessment, and it protects CtQ domain 10. Other controls also run through conduct, but among them safety is the only one bound to external reporting intervals and the only one that links events from different phases, since a complication seen in follow-up may come from a decision made at surgery. Its review is held at least once a month, and the record of each implanted unit stays current for as long as the participant is followed.

Continuous improvement closes the cycle because its question, what this investigation taught the site about how it runs investigations, can be fully answered only once conduct is complete. Correction does not wait for it. Corrective and preventive action runs from the first case, and a weakness found in one investigation reaches the others that the site is running through preventive action, without waiting for this one to end. The closing phase consolidates what the corrections and the risk register recorded during conduct and turns it into changes to the site’s standing procedures, so the lessons do not depend on the memory of people who may have left, as DR10 requires. The Post-Investigation Debrief and Lessons Record (PIDLR) holds the debrief and its lessons (Appendix X), and the next investigation starts from the procedures that Phase 7 leaves in place.
caption: Figure 4.1. The seven phases of the quality lifecycle in three groups, with the transversal safety stream and, for each phase, its objective, its actions and checks, and the condition that closes it.
